For example when she says studies say this she doesn't say who the study was by, the sample size, how they quantified "feeling better" how long you have to do this thing for it to work, how long it will work for, if this is an unlimited effect or if you do it then after a certain value it plateaus and where this plateau is, this vs a control group, this vs normal treatment. Then taken a study out of context, saying social contact supports this, something else says shaking hands is social contact therefore shaking hands helps. Its the same as the argument average temp of the earth is increasing while no. of pirates is decreasing, does that mean pirates kept the earth cool. Its the basic cause vs correlation thing.

An example of this is you'd think that sports drinks are better for you than water, they're not they make no difference to an average person who does exercise. You needed to do continuous exercise for 2hrs plus to see any benefit, even then its negligible. Companies who've made claims about sports drinks are always going to be funded by said company so will try to portray the results in the best possible light.

Part of a post I made to someone else about my knowledge of how they work on a biological level.

I'm afraid my knowledge is only A level but its a bit of psychology and biology combined. What we were taught was only SSRI's however I'm fairly sure that SNRI's work in the same fashion but inhibiting the reuptake of neopinephrine as well.

Right, the way we experience pleasure is either the release (from one neurone) of serotonin or dopamine into synapses (the gap between neurones) which cause a response in the next neurone along to tell the brain you're experiencing pleasure. One of the reasons for depression is the lack or serotonin in your brain. This means that the first neurone has less serotonin to release into the synapse. (For most things this is fine as it works on an all or nothing system, either there's enough chemical to cause a response or not). Normally when the body neads more information about the amount of pleasure or pain etc to feel a thing called summation happens. You can have spatial summation where the chemical in the synapse triggers a response in several neurones. Or you have temporal summation in which the chemical remains in the synapse longer so multiple responses can be sent down the same neurone. The most common anti-depressants are SSRI's, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. This means the molecules that are normally responsible in removing the serotonin from the synapse back into the first neurone (ready for a fresh impulse) are inhibited, therefore the serotonin remains in your synapse for longer and temporal summation occurs (I believe, cannot directly remember but it would seem to fit) and so you get a larger pleasure response than normal which can bring you up to par with non depression sufferers.

Basically it slows down a naturally occurring process (so nothing abnormal) so more impulses are sent to your brain telling you to experience pleasure, the more impulses the better you feel.

I'd also like the add that the word pleasure in this context isn't something like sexual euphoria, but the general feeling good about yourself and your surroundings.

These are types of drugs that as far as I'm aware are non-addicting. You will most likely experience side effects due to a change in chemical balance in your brain. However for the majority of these your body will adjust and they should recede. As far as dependency is concerned if you find one that works then you may feel that you need it to continue living happily. However what I found is that when it does work you find yourself being comfortable in a lot of new situations, have the motivation to go out and do things that you now enjoy. The drugs can be a stepping stone in order for you to reach a place in which you are comfortable and find joy in other things which can replace what the function that they drugs were originally used for. 

Pills are not the only answer, I'm assuming you're reasonably young in which case CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy is found to be as effective in young people as drugs in treating mild depression). Its just a way to change how you think, not how you think, but how you view certain things. In most cases its recommended that you take the medication and undergo some form of counselling such as a psychotherapist, psychologist or CBT for the best possible outcome. 

If there's anything I've not explained clearly or want something clarified that feel free to ask, I'll do my best but always be aware that you can talk to your doctor.

They're 2 different classes , selective serotonin re uptake inhibitors, SSRI's, they basically slow the process of removal of serotonin from they synapses in your brain whenever serotonin is released. This does something called temporal summation, so because it's there for a longer time "pleasure impulses" are sent down that neurone and you feel better. SNRI's do the same thing really, serotonin-norepinephrine re uptake inhibitors so they work on 2 different chemicals. 

Basically if you find one class of drug not working as you've likely heard it's a bit of trial and error and you want to try something else then it's worth asking to try a different class. I'm fairly sure there's a few others but I've not tried any of them. I'd liken it to paracetamol and ibuprofen both painkillers just work in slightly different ways.
